items.title: Plane and pipe Couette–Poiseuille verification
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

references.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6: Fluid Mechanics
David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 2: The Navier–Stokes Equation
Shreyas Mandre, Fluid Dynamics Lecture Notes, Chapter 3: One-dimensional flows

items.title: Vortex topology and global-Bernoulli counterexamples
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Let $D=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0\}$, let $\rho_0>0$, $p_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\kappa\ne0$. On $D$ define

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. Both $\operatorname{div}u_v=0$ and $\Delta u_v=0$ on $D$, and the pointwise identity

$$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Separately, for $\Omega_0\ne0$ set $u_s=(-\Omega_0y,\Omega_0x,0)$ and $p_s=p_0+\rho_0\Omega_0^2r^2/2$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This smooth steady field is divergence-free and satisfies the same constant-density equation for every $\nu>0$. Its Bernoulli quantity $B=|u_s|^2/2+p_s/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega_0^2r^2$ is constant on each circular streamline but varies with $r$. Thus a common Bernoulli constant is not implied for all steady constant-density flows. This example does not contradict a Bernoulli theorem that assumes an irrotational field or a separate barotropic model. Under SI interpretation, $r$ is in metres, the velocities in metres per second, $\kappa$ in square metres per second, $\Omega_0$ in inverse seconds, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_0$ in pascals.

references.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6: Fluid Mechanics
David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 1: Introduction and Inviscid Flows

items.title: Exterior sphere Stokes solution, force and decay-class uniqueness
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. On the exterior domain $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ put $s=U\cdot x$ and define

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

This field is $C^2$ up to the spherical boundary from the exterior, $p$ is $C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u\to U$ uniformly in direction as $r\to\infty$. It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. For $n=x/a$ on $S_a=\{x:|x|=a\}$, put $D u=(\partial_j u_i)_{i,j}$ and form the stress $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(Du+(Du)^{\mathsf T})$. The formal resultant with this sphere orientation is

$$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Here the velocity is $C^2$ and pressure $C^1$ locally up to $S_a$, the displayed bounds hold uniformly in direction, and pressure is normalized by its limit $p_\infty$. The claim is for the Stokes equations only; it gives no finite-Reynolds-number error bound or exterior Navier–Stokes existence result. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_\infty$ in pascals, and the resultant in newtons.

references.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6: Fluid Mechanics
David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 2: The Navier–Stokes Equation

items.title: Barotropic Kelvin and Bernoulli with exact hypotheses
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. A streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ with $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

references.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6: Fluid Mechanics
David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 1: Introduction and Inviscid Flows

items.title: Formal constant-density incompressible Euler system
items.design_state: Step 1 local prerequisite added to close the exact formal Euler-system interface required by thm-fd-x13; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

items.title: Exterior potential sphere and zero ideal force
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and on $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ define $n=x/r$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. Then $u,p$ are smooth in the exterior and up to $r=a$, $u\to U$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction at infinity, and $u\cdot n=0$ on $r=a$. The pair solves $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the steady formal constant-density incompressible Euler system. Its boundary condition is impermeable slip/no-through: $u$ is generally nonzero tangent to the sphere, so this is not a no-slip solution. For the formal Euler stress $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from the center into the exterior, the exact resultant is

$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$

The theorem concerns only this explicit inviscid mathematical model; it asserts neither a viscous zero-drag result nor an observed force. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U,u$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_\infty$ in pascals.

references.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6: Fluid Mechanics
David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 1: Introduction and Inviscid Flows

items.title: Plane and pipe Couette–Poiseuille verification — formal worked fields
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement: Set $h=2$, $V_0=0$, $V_1=1$, $G=4$, $\mu=2$, $\rho_0=1$, and $p_0=0$ in the plane-channel model. The profile is $v(y)=\frac52y-y^2$ for $0\le y\le2$, with flux $Q_{\rm ch}=7/3$ and fixed-coordinate wall shear components $\sigma_{xy}(0)=5$ and $\sigma_{xy}(2)=-3$. In the pipe, set $a=1$, $G=8$, $\mu=2$, $\rho_0=1$, and $p_0=0$; the profile is $w(r)=1-r^2$ on the unit disk and its volume flux is $Q_{\rm pipe}=\pi/2$. These are exact infinite or fully developed formal solutions within the theorem's one-dimensional ansatz.

items.title: Vortex topology and global-Bernoulli counterexamples — formal worked fields
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement: For $\kappa=1$, $\rho_0=2$, $p_0=0$, and $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0$, the vortex is $u_v=(-y/r^2,x/r^2,0)$ with pressure $p_v=-1/r^2$. Its circle of radius $R=2$ has circulation $2\pi$. Separately, for solid rotation take $\Omega_0=1$, $\rho_0=2$, and $p_0=0$; then $u_s=(-y,x,0)$ and $p_s=r^2$, and its Bernoulli quantity is $B=r^2$. Thus circles of distinct radii have distinct Bernoulli values.

items.title: Exterior sphere Stokes solution, force and uniqueness — formal worked field
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement:
Take $a=\mu=\rho_0=1$, $p_\infty=0$, and $U=e_z=(0,0,1)$ on $r>1$. With $s=z$, the exact field and pressure are

$$u=A(r)e_z+B(r)zx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3}{4r}-\frac{1}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3}{4r^3}+\frac{3}{4r^5},\qquad p=-\frac{3z}{2r^3}.$$

It has zero velocity on the unit sphere, tends uniformly to $e_z$, and its formal stress resultant with $n=x$ is $6\pi e_z$. The theorem's uniqueness conclusion applies among fields in its stated uniform decay class.

items.title: Exact viscous diffusion layer and material-circulation decay — formal worked fields
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement: For the wall layer take $\nu=U=1$. At time $t=1$ and distance $y=2$ from the wall, the exact solution obeys $|u(1,2)|=E(1)\le e^{-1}$. In the separate periodic example, take $L_x=4$, $L_y=2\pi$, $L_z=1$, $m=k=1$, $A=2$, $c=1$, and $b=\pi/2$. Then $\alpha=kb=\pi/2$ and the smooth material ellipse in the Statement has circulation $\Gamma(t)=2C_{\pi/2}e^{-t}$, where $C_{\pi/2}=\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\sin((\pi/2)\cos\theta)\,d\theta>0$. Its circulation strictly decreases between times $0$ and $1$.

items.title: Barotropic Kelvin and Bernoulli with exact hypotheses — formal worked solution
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement: Let $I=\mathbb R$, $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $P(q)=q$ for $q>0$, $\rho_{\rm ref}=1$, $\rho(t,x)=1$, $V=0$, and $u(t,x)=(1,0,0)$. These fields solve the barotropic Euler system. The enthalpy is $h(q)=\log q$, so the Bernoulli quantity is the constant $1/2$. The closed loop $X(t,s)=(\cos(2\pi s)+t,\sin(2\pi s),0)$ is material and has circulation $0$ for every $t$.

items.title: Exterior potential sphere and zero ideal force — formal worked field
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; conditional supplier/readiness status recorded separately in batch-6 notes.
items.statement: Choose $a=\rho_0=1$, $p_\infty=0$, and $U=e_x=(1,0,0)$. For $r>1$ let $\phi=x(1+1/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=(1-|u|^2)/2$. On the unit sphere, $u=(3/2)(e_x-n_xn)$ and $p=-5/8+(9/8)n_x^2$. The pressure is unchanged by $n\mapsto-n$, so the pressure-only formal resultant is zero.
